lines.text:
Vertical Wilderness — Reading the Mountain

A mountain is a vertical ecosystem — a landscape where climate, vegetation, and wildlife change dramatically with every few hundred metres of elevation. To climb a mountain is to travel through multiple environments in a single day, from temperate forest to arctic tundra, and to encounter vocabulary that is both specific and immediately useful.

The anatomy of a mountain is defined by its landforms. The summit — or peak — is the highest point. A ridge connects peaks along a narrow crest. A cliff is a vertical or near-vertical rock face. A valley lies between mountains. A slope is any inclined surface. A boulder is a large, isolated rock. A ledge is a narrow horizontal shelf on a cliff face. A crevasse is a deep crack in ice or rock — invisible under snow, it is one of the mountain's greatest dangers. A plateau is a flat, elevated area.

Vegetation follows altitude. At lower elevations, pine trees dominate — their bark rough, their roots gripping thin soil. Ferns and moss carpet the forest floor. Wildflowers colour the alpine meadow — the open grassland above the forest. Shrubs and lichen survive where trees cannot. The tree line — the altitude above which trees stop growing — marks a dramatic boundary. Above it, only the hardiest plants survive: low-growing, wind-resistant, adapted to frost and thin air.

Wildlife adapts to altitude and season. An eagle circles above the ridge. A mountain goat navigates vertical rock with astonishing agility. A bear forages in the valley. A deer moves through the tree line at dawn. A wolf hunts in the higher meadows. A marmot — a large, social rodent — whistles a warning from a boulder. A hawk surveys from a ledge. An owl hunts at dusk. A fox adapts to every elevation. A mountain lion — solitary and rarely seen — controls the largest territory.

Mountain weather is unpredictable and potentially lethal. Snow can fall in any month at altitude. Fog obscures trails and landmarks. Wind accelerates on ridges and exposed slopes. Cloud descends without warning. Lightning strikes exposed summits. Frost forms overnight. Hail arrives with little notice. But the rewards are equally dramatic: a sunrise that illuminates an entire range, a sunset that turns snow orange, a rainbow arching across a valley.

The equipment a hiker carries reflects the mountain's demands. A backpack holds everything. Hiking boots provide ankle support and grip. A trekking pole aids balance on steep terrain. A water bottle prevents dehydration. A compass and a map are essential — GPS signals can fail at altitude. A headlamp lights the trail before dawn and after dark. A tent and a sleeping bag provide overnight shelter. A rope is carried for technical sections.

Activities on a mountain range from gentle to extreme: hiking on marked trails, climbing on rock or ice, camping in designated areas, skiing and snowboarding on winter slopes, photography of landscapes and wildlife, bird watching at the tree line, fishing in mountain streams, trail running on ridgelines, and stargazing from high-altitude camps where light pollution is absent.

The mountain does not care whether you are prepared. Its indifference is what makes preparation essential — and what makes the summit, when you reach it, feel earned.

lines.text: There is no universally agreed height that separates a mountain from a hill. In the UK, the traditional boundary is 2,000 feet (610m) — below that, it's a hill. The term 'fell' is used in northern England (Lake District). 'Munro' = a Scottish mountain over 3,000 feet (914m). 'Ben' = Scottish word for mountain peak (e.g. Ben Nevis).
lines.name: There is no universally agreed height that separates a mountain from a hill. In the UK, the traditional boundary is 2,000 feet (610m) — below that, it's a hill. The term 'fell' is used in northern England (Lake District). 'Munro' = a Scottish mountain over 3,000 feet (914m). 'Ben' = Scottish word for mountain peak (e.g. Ben Nevis).

lines.text: 'Walking' = general term, any distance. 'Hiking' = walking in the countryside, usually on trails, for exercise or pleasure. 'Trekking' = a long, multi-day hike, often in remote areas. 'Rambling' (BrE) = walking in the countryside for pleasure (ramblers = hikers). 'Fell walking' = hiking on fells in northern England.

lines.text: In England and Wales, the Countryside and Rights of Way Act (2000) gives the public the right to walk across certain open land — mountains, moors, heaths, and downs — even if it's privately owned. Scotland has even broader access rights. In the US, public trails exist but most private land is off-limits.

lines.text: Above about 2,500m, the air has less oxygen. This can cause altitude sickness: headache, nausea, dizziness, and shortness of breath. Severe cases can be fatal. The treatment is to descend immediately. Climbers on very high mountains acclimatise by climbing slowly and spending rest days at each altitude.

lines.text: 'Despite' + noun/gerund: 'despite the dangerous weather', 'despite being exhausted.' 'Although' + full clause: 'although the weather was dangerous.' Never *'despite + subject + verb.' 'In spite of' follows 'despite' rules: 'in spite of the conditions.' This is a persistent B2 error.

lines.text: 'For' + duration: 'for four hours', 'for two days.' 'Since' + point in time: 'since dawn', 'since 6 a.m.', 'since we left the camp.' Never *'since four hours.' Present perfect continuous + for emphasises ongoing effort: 'We've been climbing for four hours' = we started four hours ago and we're still climbing.

lines.text: Modal verbs (can, could, will, would, shall, should, may, might, must) are followed by the bare infinitive — no 's', no 'to': 'can climb', 'should prepare', 'must carry.' Never *'can climbs' or *'can to climb.' The modal itself never changes form: 'he can', 'she can', 'it can' — no third-person 's.'
